data_note: Revised 2026-11-15: the FY2025 (and FY2023/FY2024) 10-Ks and 10-Qs in research/WEC/Extracted/ DO contain full narrative text -- Item 1 Business, Item 1A Risk Factors, and Item 7 MD&A -- not just inline-XBRL tag dumps as a prior pass of this file incorrectly stated. This analysis is now grounded primarily in the FY2025 Form 10-K's own language (Item 1 Business starting ~line 7419, Item 1A Risk Factors ~line 7872, Item 7 MD&A ~line 8382 of WEC_Annual_FY2025.txt), supplemented by web research for developments more recent than the 10-K (Q3 2026 earnings, the expanded 2027-2031 capital plan, the Oracle/PSCW tariff lawsuit, and the Moody's WPS outlook change).
overview: WEC Energy Group is a Milwaukee, Wisconsin-based diversified holding company (incorporated in Wisconsin in 1981, renamed from Wisconsin Energy in 2015 after acquiring Integrys) with six reportable segments: Wisconsin (electric and natural gas utilities WE, WPS, WG, and UMERC), Illinois (natural gas utilities PGL and NSG serving Chicago and northern suburbs), Other states (natural gas utilities MERC in Minnesota and MGU in Michigan), Electric transmission (an approximately 60% equity interest in American Transmission Company, a FERC-regulated transmission company operating in WI/MI/IL/MN), Non-utility energy infrastructure (We Power, which leases generation to WE; Bluewater, Michigan gas storage; and WECI, renewable generation interests), and Corporate and other. The company earns cost-of-service, rate-base regulated returns set by the Wisconsin PSC, Illinois ICC, Michigan PSC, Minnesota PUC, and FERC, with Wisconsin representing roughly 71% of consolidated utility operating revenue in FY2025.

business_model.summary: WEC's subsidiaries recover prudently incurred operating costs and capital investment plus an allowed ROE set by state regulators and FERC; authorized ROEs in FY2025 ranged from 9.38% (PGL/NSG, Illinois ICC) to 9.86% (UMERC and MGU, Michigan PSC), with WE/WPS/WG at 9.80% (Wisconsin PSC) and MERC at 9.65% (Minnesota PUC) -- and the company has proposed a materially higher 10.48%-10.98% ROE band with a 57% equity ratio specifically for Very Large Customer (VLC/data-center) tariffs. Several jurisdictions use earnings-sharing mechanisms that require refunds to customers if a utility earns above its authorized ROE. In FY2025, segment net income attributed to common shareholders was: Wisconsin $1,054.8M (68%), non-utility energy infrastructure $411.1M (26%, driven heavily by production tax credits from renewable acquisitions), electric transmission/ATC $147.6M (9%), Illinois $122.1M (8%, depressed by a $205M Q4 2025 charge tied to a PGL/NSG settlement with the Illinois AG over UEA/QIP rider reconciliations), other states $60.8M (4%), and corporate and other a $(238.9)M loss (-15%), summing to $1,557.5M total. Earnings growth is driven mechanically by rate-base growth (capex) and rate-case outcomes rather than sales volume, with a newly material driver being contracted 'Very Large Customer' (hyperscale data center) load.

revenue_streams.name: Electric transmission (ATC, equity method, not consolidated revenue)
Non-utility energy infrastructure (We Power leases, Bluewater storage, WECI renewables -- ~26% of net income via PTCs, modest consolidated revenue)

business_model.customer_type: Predominantly B2C/residential and commercial retail utility customers (FY2025: 1.70M electric and 1.55M+1.06M+0.44M gas customers across Wisconsin/Illinois/other states), plus wholesale, municipal/cooperative, and a fast-growing 'Very Large Customer' (hyperscale data center) segment
business_model.geographic_mix: Wisconsin electric ~90% of electric revenue / Wisconsin gas ~44% of gas revenue (combined ~71% of total utility revenue); Illinois gas ~42.5% of gas revenue (~18% of total); Minnesota gas ~8.3% and Michigan gas ~5.2% of gas revenue; Michigan electric ~3.1% and FERC wholesale ~6.9% of electric revenue; all revenue US-domestic, no FX exposure

competitive_position.market_position: Exclusive franchised provider of electric and/or natural gas distribution service under indeterminate permits and municipal boundary agreements (Wisconsin) and franchises (Michigan) -- per the 10-K, 'not a market-share business' for core transmission and distribution, though the filing explicitly discloses competition in electric wholesale/municipal sales and in natural gas supply/transportation choice

moat_factors.description: Per Item 1, electric utilities operate under indeterminate permits and boundary agreements (Wisconsin) and municipal franchises (Michigan); natural gas utilities hold similar indeterminate permits -- no realistic competitive entry for core distribution, though the 10-K's Competition section notes electric utilities do compete with other utilities for municipal/cooperative sales and with marketers for wholesale business
Forward-looking test years, fuel/GCRM cost-recovery riders, and earnings-sharing mechanisms (WE, WPS, WG) allow fairly timely recovery of a large capital program, per Item 1.E Regulation
~60% equity interest in American Transmission Company (ATC) and ~75% of ATC Holdco provide FERC formula-rate earnings largely insulated from state rate-case risk

moat_factors.factor: First-mover position in Wisconsin data-center/VLC contracts
moat_factors.description: Microsoft's >$20B Mount Pleasant-area investment (up to 2.6 GW of load in the Milwaukee-to-Chicago corridor through 2030) and Vantage Data Centers' Port Washington campus (1.3 GW, with potential for a further 2.2 GW) create a large contracted growth pipeline; WE has filed proposed VLC and Bespoke Resources tariffs with the PSCW requiring customers to pay cancellation/reimbursement obligations, which the company argues protects both WEC and ratepayers

weaknesses: Concentrated exposure to Wisconsin regulatory outcomes (PSCW) given ~71% of utility revenue and 68% of segment net income from that state in FY2025

Natural gas retail choice already exists in Michigan (capped at 10% of UMERC retail load, excluding the Tilden iron-ore mine) and Illinois (PGL/NSG retain the distribution charge so net-income impact is immaterial per the 10-K, but it shows the commodity itself is contestable)

Illinois regulatory friction: the ICC's November 2023 rate order disallowed certain PGL/NSG capital costs (causing Q4 2023 impairments and a pause on the pipe-replacement program), and in Q4 2025 PGL/NSG took a $205.0 million pre-tax charge tied to a proposed settlement with the Illinois Attorney General resolving open UEA/QIP rider reconciliation proceedings

Reliance on large, lumpy data-center load concentration (Microsoft, Vantage, Oracle-linked tenants) that creates counterparty credit and project-execution risk, as evidenced by the Oracle/PSCW tariff lawsuit
Wisconsin Utility Holding Company Act anti-takeover provisions (25% non-utility asset cap; PSCW pre-approval required for >=10% share acquisitions) could deter a premium-paying acquirer, per Item 1A

growth_drivers: Data center / 'Very Large Customer' load growth in Wisconsin -- per the FY2025 10-K, Microsoft's planned >$20B of southern Wisconsin data-center investment (up to 2.6 GW through 2030 in the Milwaukee-to-Chicago corridor) and Vantage Data Centers' Port Washington campus (1.3 GW, potentially expanding to 3.5 GW total); WE has filed proposed VLC and Bespoke Resources tariffs with the PSCW

Capital plan of ~$37.5 billion (2026-2030, ~$33.4B regulated utility + ~$4.1B WEC's share of ATC), split per the 10-K into ~$12.6B regulated renewables (3,850 MW solar, 2,130 MW battery, 555 MW wind), ~$5.4B efficient gas-fired generation (3,300 MW of CTs plus 180 MW of RICE units), ~$2.9B battery storage, and ~$7.1B/$4.7B gas/electric distribution reliability spend; management has since outlined a larger $47.5B plan for 2027-2031 on the Q3 2026 call

Rate base growth translating to management's long-term EPS growth guidance of 7-8%, raised toward 7-9%+ commentary alongside the expanded capital plan, with management expecting the upper half of the range starting in 2028
Transmission build-out via ATC, including >$2 billion of projects tied to data-center-driven load growth

Generation transition economics -- coal used only as backup fuel by end of 2030 and eliminated as an energy source by end of 2032 (Columbia Units 1/2 to continue operating through at least 2029 with ongoing evaluation of a gas conversion), replaced with new gas, solar, wind and battery storage that supports continued rate-base investment
LNG storage expansion (WE's approved 2 Bcf facility plus a proposed ~4 Bcf of additional capacity) to meet peak winter gas demand without new interstate pipeline capacity

Continued residential/commercial retail load growth -- the 10-K forecasts 2026 Wisconsin retail electric sales up 1.6% (including VLCs) versus roughly flat excluding VLCs; Q3 2026 results showed electric deliveries (ex-iron-ore mine/VLC) up 3.3% and residential up 5.1%, a positive surprise versus the historically flat-to-low-growth utility demand backdrop

business.description: Per Item 1A, WE is incurring significant engineering, design, and equipment costs ahead of PSCW approval of the VLC/Bespoke Resources tariffs; if projects are canceled (e.g., due to lower-than-forecast demand or failed approvals), WE may face contract cancellation penalties, impairments, and may not recover these costs in rates. The 10-K explicitly flags this as 'concentration of business with a small number of customers in an industry based on emerging technologies, including AI and machine learning'

business.risk: Execution risk on a record capital program
business.description: Item 1A cites supply chain disruptions (including solar panel shortages), tariffs, inflation, contractor performance, and permitting/siting risk; regulators could deem resulting cost overruns imprudent and disallow recovery, as occurred with the ICC's 2023 PGL/NSG disallowance

business.risk: Legal/regulatory challenge to large-load tariff protections
business.description: Oracle sued the Wisconsin PSC over credit-requirement provisions in the VLC tariff designed to protect ratepayers from data-center cost shifting; an adverse ruling could weaken ratepayer protections or complicate contracting (web-sourced; not yet reflected in the FY2025 10-K)

Item 1A discloses the company has been subject to attempted cyberattacks and depends on sophisticated IT/OT systems across generation, transmission, and distribution; a successful intrusion could disrupt service, and related costs/litigation may not be fully recoverable in rates or covered by insurance

A new FY2025 risk factor: WEC's and its vendors' use of AI (including generative AI) carries risks of bias, IP infringement, data privacy, and new regulatory scrutiny, and related investment may not be recoverable through regulatory proceedings

Item 1A notes continued cost declines in distributed solar, storage, and self-generation could erode fixed-cost recovery and market share over time, and that co-location of generation near data centers could affect generation planning and cost recovery

financial.risk: Rising debt load / credit metric pressure
financial.description: Moody's moved Wisconsin Public Service's outlook to negative (Nov 2025) citing deteriorating financial ratios tied to the capital plan's scale (web-sourced); Item 1A separately flags that a credit-rating downgrade could raise borrowing costs, trigger collateral postings, and limit funding sources

Item 1A: the company relies on debt and equity issuance (including commercial paper backed by bank credit facilities) to fund capex not covered by operating cash flow; rising rates, rating downgrades, covenant breaches, or stressed capital markets could raise financing costs or limit access, potentially constraining the dividend

A record capital plan is likely to require continued equity issuance that can dilute EPS growth if not matched by rate-base returns; AFUDC/CWIP growth during construction delays cash recovery, which Item 1A notes may require additional debt/equity issuance

Item 1A flags use of derivatives (swaps, options, futures) to hedge natural gas and coal price risk, with potential financial losses if counterparties default or hedges fail to offset exposure as intended

regulatory.description: Wisconsin PSC approved materially smaller increases than requested in the 2027-2028 cases for We Energies (~3.9%/3.5% vs. a larger ask) and Wisconsin Public Service (~0.3%/2.9%), with WPS staff also recommending a lower authorized ROE (9.50% vs. requested 9.90%, versus the FY2025-authorized 9.80% disclosed in the 10-K) (web-sourced; figures not yet in a filed 10-K)

Per Item 1A/MD&A, the ICC's November 2023 order disallowed certain PGL capital costs (Q4 2023 impairment, paused pipe-replacement spending) and a February 2025 ICC order requires PGL to retire all cast/ductile iron pipe under 36 inches by January 1, 2035 (with civil-penalty exposure for noncompliance); a Q4 2025 PGL/NSG settlement with the Illinois AG over UEA/QIP rider reconciliations resulted in a $205.0 million pre-tax charge, subject to ICC approval

WE's proposed VLC and Bespoke Resources tariffs are designed so VLC-related generation, distribution, and transmission costs are not subsidized by other customers; regulators rejected a prior WE proposal to share some data-center infrastructure costs with general ratepayers (web-sourced), raising the bar for future large-load deal economics

Item 1A discusses the July 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), which modified IRA clean-energy tax credits -- including new 'beginning of construction' rules and restrictions tied to prohibited foreign entities -- creating uncertainty for WECI's solar/wind PTC/ITC transferability sales and potential rating-agency treatment of related metrics (e.g., FFO-to-debt)

Per Item 1A, a late-2025 executive order directed the DOE to issue orders keeping certain coal plants running for grid reliability despite utility retirement plans, which could disrupt WEC's capital plan execution; separately, parts of southeastern Wisconsin were reclassified to 'serious' ozone nonattainment in Dec 2024 (now stayed to 'moderate' pending a Seventh Circuit appeal), which could tighten future permitting

Net-carbon-neutral-by-2050 goal, with coal as backup fuel only by 2030 and fully eliminated by 2032, requires large replacement capex in gas (including LNG) and renewables; evolving EPA deregulatory/regulatory actions and GHG litigation risk (per Item 1A) are a swing factor

macro.description: Item 1A: electric demand peaks in summer (cooling) and natural gas in winter (heating); decoupling mechanisms (PGL, NSG, MERC) mitigate but do not eliminate weather-driven earnings variability. Favorable weather was cited as a driver of the Q3 2026 guidance raise, implying downside risk in a milder/more normal weather year
As a high-dividend-yield, capital-intensive utility, WEC's valuation multiple tends to compress when long-term rates rise and investors rotate out of yield-sensitive sectors

macro.risk: Coal and natural gas supply chain exposure
macro.description: Item 1A notes coal is sourced from Wyoming/Pennsylvania mines via owned/leased unit trains (51% of 2026's projected 8.9 million tons under fixed-price contract), with rail congestion, derailments, or supplier financial stress a risk to fuel supply; natural gas and purchased power costs are largely pass-through via fuel/GCRM cost-recovery mechanisms, limiting but not eliminating margin risk

macro_factors.industry_outlook: US regulated electric/gas utilities are experiencing a historic re-acceleration in demand growth after two decades of flat load, driven by AI/data-center buildouts, electrification and industrial reshoring; Wisconsin specifically has become a focal point for hyperscale data-center investment (Microsoft, Vantage), giving WEC an outsized rate-base growth opportunity versus its historical profile. The FY2025 10-K separately discloses retail natural gas choice already operating in Michigan and Illinois and ongoing electrification/decarbonization pressure on gas distribution (e.g., Chicago decarbonization efforts, state bans on gas hookups under consideration)
macro_factors.cyclicality: Low-to-moderate; regulated utility earnings are largely insulated from economic cycles via cost-of-service recovery, though Item 1A notes commercial/industrial demand (including large data-center customers) introduces a new source of demand variability tied to AI/technology-sector capital spending cycles
macro_factors.interest_rate_sensitivity: Moderate-to-high; capital-intensive business model with large, continuous external financing needs (debt and equity) makes WEC sensitive to rate levels (Item 1A explicitly lists rising rates as a risk to results and to the regulated subsidiaries' ability to earn approved returns), and as a high-yield equity it is also sensitive to relative yield-seeking flows
key_input_costs: Coal (Wyoming/Pennsylvania mines, largely pass-through via fuel rules)
Natural gas (fuel and gas-distribution cost of sales, largely pass-through)
Construction materials/labor and solar-panel/tariff exposure for the capital program
Financing costs (debt and equity capital for the $37.5-47.5B five-year plan)

recent_developments.event: Q3 2026 results: net income $389.3M ($1.18/diluted share) vs. $0.83 a year earlier; nine-month EPS $4.54. Company raised and narrowed full-year 2026 EPS guidance to $5.60-$5.64 (from $5.51-$5.61), citing favorable weather and Very Large Customer-supported capital investment; retail electric deliveries (ex-iron-ore-mine and VLCs) up 3.3%, residential usage up 5.1%

Management outlined a prospective $47.5 billion capital plan for 2027-2031 (up from the $37.5B 2026-2030 plan disclosed in the FY2025 10-K), targeting roughly a 13%+ asset-base CAGR and raising long-term EPS growth guidance toward the 7-9%+ range through 2031

PGL and NSG agreed to the terms of a proposed settlement with the Illinois Attorney General resolving all open UEA/QIP rider reconciliation proceedings (including 2017-2023), recording a $205.0 million pre-tax charge to income in Q4 2025 through an impairment to PP&E and a revenue reduction; the settlement requires ICC approval

In March 2025, WE filed a PSCW application for VLC and Bespoke Resources tariffs designed so data-center customers directly bear the generation, distribution, and transmission costs built to serve them, rather than shifting costs to other customers; WE is incurring significant pre-approval engineering/design costs and requires VLCs to sign payment and cancellation agreements

Dispute over VLC credit-protection terms: the Wisconsin PSC set a credit-rating threshold for data-center operators to shield ratepayers from cost-shift risk; Oracle (tenant/counterparty tied to the Port Washington/Vantage data center) sued the PSC in Ozaukee County Circuit Court to overturn the requirement; CEO Scott Lauber said the dispute does not threaten the project timeline and that collateral already held covers near-term risk

We Energies and Wisconsin Public Service each filed 2027-2028 rate cases seeking roughly 9-15% cumulative residential increases; after staff review and commission deliberation, the PSC approved materially smaller increases (We Energies ~3.9%/3.5%; WPS ~0.3%/2.9%) than requested, with WPS staff also recommending a lower authorized ROE (9.50% vs. 9.90% requested, versus 9.80% currently authorized per the FY2025 10-K)

WEC raised its five-year capital plan to $37.5 billion after Microsoft's Mount Pleasant data center expansion added incremental load forecast; management signaled on the May 2026 earnings call that 'another announcement' of a large-load customer was likely in the following months
Moody's revised the outlook on subsidiary Wisconsin Public Service to negative, citing deteriorating financial ratios associated with the scale of the capital investment program

A presidential executive order directed the DOE to issue orders keeping certain coal plants running for grid reliability despite utilities' retirement plans; WEC continues to plan retirement of ~900 MW of additional coal capacity (OCPP Units 7/8, Weston Unit 3) by end of 2031 while Columbia Units 1/2 continue operating through at least 2029

guidance.as_of: Q3 2026 earnings release/call (2026-10-29); five-year capital plan figures per FY2025 Form 10-K updated by subsequent management commentary

items.notes: Raised and narrowed from prior $5.51-$5.61; reflects favorable weather and continued Very Large Customer-supported capital investment; assumes normal weather for Q4

items.target: 7-8% (management commentary pointing toward 7-9%+ with the expanded $47.5B plan)
items.notes: Management said it expects to be in the upper half of the 7-8% guidance range starting in 2028; a Q3 2026 call summary points to 7-9%+ annual EPS growth under the larger 2027-2031 capital plan

items.target: ~$37.5B (2026-2030, per FY2025 10-K: ~$33.4B regulated utility + ~$4.1B WEC's share of ATC) / ~$47.5B (2027-2031, outlined on Q3 2026 call)
items.notes: 10-K detail: ~$12.6B regulated renewables (3,850 MW solar/2,130 MW battery/555 MW wind), ~$5.4B gas-fired generation, ~$2.9B BESS, ~$7.1B gas distribution reliability, ~$4.7B electric distribution reliability; the subsequent 2027-2031 plan represents a further large step-up driven by data-center/large-load demand
Figure from a Q3 2026 earnings-call summary tied to the expanded $47.5B capital plan; not yet independently confirmed against the primary investor presentation
Consistent with WEC's historical policy of annual dividend increases roughly in line with EPS growth

items.target: Up to 2.6 GW in the Milwaukee-to-Chicago corridor through 2030 (Microsoft) plus 1.3 GW at Port Washington with potential expansion to 3.5 GW total (Vantage), per the FY2025 10-K; some web sources cite a combined figure up to ~3.9-7.4 GW
items.notes: Driven primarily by Microsoft's Mount Pleasant-area campus and Vantage Data Centers' Port Washington campus; sources disagree on exact MW/GW figures and scope, so treat combined totals as directional

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Scott Lauber has emphasized that the Oracle credit-rating dispute does not threaten the Port Washington data-center project timeline and that existing collateral already protects the company and ratepayers; he has also signaled that additional large-load customer announcements are likely. The FY2025 10-K frames corporate strategy around reliability, operating efficiency, financial discipline, environmental stewardship, exceptional customer care, and safety, with the capital plan as the primary vehicle; management frames the expanded capital plan and raised long-term growth guidance as underpinned by contracted VLC load, constructive (if trimmed-back) regulatory outcomes, and continued above-trend retail load growth.

bull_case: Rare acceleration in rate-base growth for a regulated utility, driven by contracted, credit-protected hyperscale data-center load (Microsoft, Vantage) that is largely insulated from weather/economic cycles

Record and still-growing five-year capital plan ($37.5B per the FY2025 10-K, stepping toward $47.5B per subsequent management commentary) provides a long runway of regulator-sanctioned earnings growth with long-term EPS growth guidance raised toward 7-9%+
Diversified multi-state regulatory footprint (WI/IL/MI/MN) plus a ~60% stake in FERC-regulated ATC transmission reduces single-regulator concentration risk relative to narrower peers
Above-trend underlying retail load growth (+3.3% ex-large-load, +5.1% residential in Q3 2026) suggests demand strength beyond just data centers, consistent with the 10-K's own 2026 sales forecast

Track record of consistent dividend growth (6.7% increase to $3.81/share in 2026) appeals to income-oriented utility investors; anti-takeover provisions in the Wisconsin Utility Holding Company Act also support management continuity for long-duration capital execution
bear_case: Heavy dependence on a handful of large-load data-center customers (Microsoft, Vantage, Oracle-linked tenants) concentrates counterparty credit and project-execution risk, as the 10-K itself flags ('concentration of business with a small number of customers in an industry based on emerging technologies') and as illustrated by the Oracle/PSCW credit-threshold lawsuit

Wisconsin regulators have recently approved materially smaller rate increases and lower authorized ROEs than requested, signaling tougher-than-hoped regulatory outcomes just as the capital plan is scaling up; Illinois regulatory friction already cost PGL/NSG a $205.0 million Q4 2025 charge and a prior 2023 ICC disallowance

Record capex funded by a mix of debt and equity raises credit-metric and dilution risk -- Moody's already moved Wisconsin Public Service's outlook to negative, citing deteriorating ratios, and the 10-K itself lists capital-markets access and rising rates as explicit risk factors
As a high-yield, capital-intensive utility, WEC's valuation and relative appeal are sensitive to a higher-for-longer interest rate environment

Coal-exit and LNG/gas buildout plans face both environmental/legal pushback (ozone nonattainment reclassification litigation, GHG/climate litigation risk per Item 1A) and a countervailing federal executive-order risk of being forced to keep coal units running longer than planned, creating two-sided regulatory/political uncertainty around the generation transition
